headline: Google spared from ad-business breakup, judge orders changes to operations
summary: A federal judge ruled Google won't have to divest its ad-tech business despite an antitrust loss, instead requiring adjustments to its practices to favor competitors.
details: The Justice Department spent years attempting to break up Google’s advertising business through two antitrust lawsuits. Both cases argued that the search giant’s grip on the digital ad economy represents an illegal monopoly.
Courts largely sided with the government in both cases, determining Google's search and ad-tech businesses were illegal monopolies. This week's ruling specifically addressed the ad-tech case.

Federal judge Leonie M. Brinkema ruled Google would be able to keep its advertising business. Instead of selling it, the search giant will be required to adjust its business practices to favor competitors, though specific details were not provided.

This outcome mirrors a 2025 ruling where Google was allowed to keep Chrome and Android despite being found an illegal monopoly in search. That case resulted in orders to end exclusive default-placement deals and share search data.

Google framed the outcome as a win, with VP Lee-Anne Mulholland expressing pleasure that the court rejected proposals to break apart tools aiding small businesses. The full written ruling will remain under seal for 14 days.
caption:
Google will not be forced to sell its massive ad-tech business following a federal antitrust ruling. Instead, the tech giant must change how it operates to boost competition.

The Justice Department spent years attempting to break up Google’s advertising business through two antitrust lawsuits. Both cases argued that the search giant’s grip on the digital ad economy represents an illegal monopoly.

Courts largely sided with the government in both cases, determining Google's search and ad-tech businesses were illegal monopolies. This week's ruling specifically addressed the ad-tech case.

Federal judge Leonie M. Brinkema ruled Google would be able to keep its advertising business. Instead of selling it, the search giant will be required to adjust its business practices to favor competitors, though specific details were not provided.

This outcome mirrors a 2025 ruling where Google was allowed to keep Chrome and Android despite being found an illegal monopoly in search. That case resulted in orders to end exclusive default-placement deals and share search data.

Google framed the outcome as a win, with VP Lee-Anne Mulholland expressing pleasure that the court rejected proposals to break apart tools aiding small businesses. The full written ruling will remain under seal for 14 days.
